front_blocks.md: Define **halogenoarene**.

back_blocks.md: A **halogenoarene** is an aromatic compound in which one or more halogen atoms are bonded directly to the benzene ring. They are also called aryl halides.

cards.back_md: A **halogenoarene** is an aromatic compound in which one or more halogen atoms are bonded directly to the benzene ring. They are also called aryl halides.

front_blocks.md: What reagents and conditions are needed to produce chlorobenzene from benzene?

back_blocks.md: Chlorine gas is bubbled into benzene at room temperature in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst. The AlCl<sub>3</sub> generates the **Cl**<sup>**+**</sup>** electrophile**, which attacks the benzene ring in an electrophilic substitution reaction.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
The chlorination of benzene requires UV light to generate the electrophile.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

The chlorination of benzene uses an anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst (halogen carrier) to generate the Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile. UV light is used for free-radical side-chain halogenation, not ring halogenation.

The chlorination of benzene requires UV light to generate the electrophile.
cards.back_md:
**False.**

The chlorination of benzene uses an anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst (halogen carrier) to generate the Cl<sup>+</sup> electrophile. UV light is used for free-radical side-chain halogenation, not ring halogenation.

front_blocks.md: In the chlorination of benzene, the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst generates the **..........** electrophile. After electrophilic attack, a **..........** atom is eliminated to restore aromaticity.

back_blocks.md: In the chlorination of benzene, the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst generates the **Cl**<sup>**+**</sup> electrophile. After electrophilic attack, a **hydrogen** atom is eliminated to restore aromaticity.

front_blocks.md: Why does chlorination of methylbenzene give two products rather than one?

back_blocks.md: The methyl group is a **2,4-directing** electron-donating group that activates the 2 and 4 positions on the ring. Electrophilic substitution therefore occurs at both positions, giving 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In the presence of excess chlorine, chlorination of methylbenzene can also occur at the 6 position.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
With excess chlorine, substitution can additionally occur at the 6 position, since the methyl group activates the 2, 4 and 6 positions by electron donation.

front_blocks.md: Define **bromobenzene**.

back_blocks.md: A **bromobenzene** is a halogenoarene produced by the electrophilic substitution of benzene with bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) in the presence of anhydrous AlBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst.

back_blocks.md: The role of the AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst in the chlorination of benzene is to generate the **electrophile (Cl**<sup>**+**</sup>**)** by reacting with Cl<sub>2</sub>, and it is described as a **halogen carrier**.

front_blocks.md: What is restored at the end of the electrophilic substitution of benzene with chlorine, and how does this happen?

back_blocks.md: **Aromaticity is restored**. A hydrogen atom is removed in the second stage of the reaction (heterolytic cleavage of the C–H bond), returning the bonding electrons to the benzene π system and regenerating the delocalised ring.

front_blocks.md: Define **partial double bond character**.

back_blocks.md: A **partial double bond character** is a property of a bond that has intermediate character between a single and a double bond, arising from electron delocalisation. In halogenoarenes, the C–X bond has partial double bond character due to lone pair overlap with the benzene π system.

cards.back_md: A **partial double bond character** is a property of a bond that has intermediate character between a single and a double bond, arising from electron delocalisation. In halogenoarenes, the C–X bond has partial double bond character due to lone pair overlap with the benzene π system.

front_blocks.md: Why are halogenoarenes much less reactive than halogenoalkanes?

back_blocks.md: In halogenoarenes, a lone pair on the halogen overlaps with the benzene π system, giving the C–X bond **partial double bond character**. This strengthens the bond and makes it very difficult to break, so nucleophilic substitution does not readily occur.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Chlorobenzene undergoes nucleophilic substitution readily at room temperature.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Chlorobenzene does not readily undergo nucleophilic substitution. Extremely harsh conditions (200°C and 200 atm pressure) are needed to replace the chlorine with a nucleophile such as OH<sup>-</sup>.

back_blocks.md: In halogenoarenes, delocalisation of a lone pair on the halogen over the benzene ring causes additional **stabilisation** of the system and **strengthens** the carbon–halogen bond.

front_blocks.md: How does chloroethane (a halogenoalkane) undergo nucleophilic substitution, and why is this different for chlorobenzene?

back_blocks.md: In chloroethane, the carbon bonded to chlorine is slightly positive, so a **nucleophile** such as OH<sup>-</sup> attacks and forms a covalent bond, displacing Cl<sup>-</sup>. In chlorobenzene, **lone pair delocalisation** into the ring strengthens the C–Cl bond so much that a nucleophile cannot break it under normal conditions.

The lone pair on the halogen in a halogenoarene interacts with the σ framework of the benzene ring.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
The lone pair on the halogen interacts with the **π system** of the benzene ring, not the σ framework. This overlap gives the C–X bond partial double bond character.

front_blocks.md: Define **chlorobenzene**.

back_blocks.md: A **chlorobenzene** is a halogenoarene formed by the electrophilic substitution of benzene with chlorine using an AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst. It is very unreactive towards nucleophilic substitution due to the partial double bond character of its C–Cl bond.

back_blocks.md: To replace the chlorine in chlorobenzene by nucleophilic substitution, conditions of **200** °C and **200** atmospheres are required.

front_blocks.md: Explain why the unreactivity of halogenoarenes can be attributed to delocalisation.

back_blocks.md: A lone pair on the halogen delocalises into the benzene π system, providing additional stabilisation of the whole molecule and giving the C–X bond **partial double bond character**. This strengthens the bond, making it harder to break. The result is that halogenoarenes are much less reactive than halogenoalkanes.
